subject: Business
title: Setting Your Walk-Away Point
description: A quick, practical guide to Setting Your Walk-Away Point.

hook.text: You told yourself you'd leave at $300K. Then they offered $290K with perks. Your resolve crumbled.

buildup.text: A walk-away point is your hard limit — the worst deal you'll accept before choosing your BATNA.

discovery.text: Write it down before the negotiation starts. Emotional pressure in the room distorts your judgment.

twist.text: Without a preset limit, you'll rationalize a bad deal in the moment. 'Close enough' costs real money.

climax.text: The walk-away point also protects you from sunk cost: you've invested time, but a bad deal is still bad.

punchline.text: Decide your limit when you're calm. Enforce it when you're not.

quiz.question: Why should you set a walk-away point before negotiating?
options: Emotions in the room distort your ability to evaluate the deal
It makes you appear more professional
It speeds up the negotiation process

details.summary: Your walk-away point, or reservation price, is the least favorable deal you would accept before choosing your alternative. Setting this boundary before negotiations begin protects against emotional drift and prevents accepting terms that are worse than walking away entirely.
details.whyItMatters: Without a preset walk-away point, negotiators get pulled into deals by the momentum of the process, sunk time, and emotional attachment.
takeaways: Set your walk-away point before negotiations begin to prevent emotional drift
The walk-away point should be slightly better than your BATNA to account for costs
Write down your limit and commit to it to resist in-the-moment pressure

faq.question: How do you calculate the right walk-away point?
faq.answer: Start with your BATNA, what you would do if negotiation fails. Add a buffer for transaction costs, time, and risk of pursuing the alternative. This gives your reservation price. Any offer above this point is better than walking away. Any offer below this point should be rejected.

faq.question: Should your walk-away point be flexible during negotiations?
faq.answer: It can adjust only if genuinely new information changes your BATNA or reveals value you did not initially consider. It should never change due to fatigue, pressure, or emotional attachment to the process. If you find yourself rationalizing a lower walk-away, that is a danger signal.
